planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from semi-hardwood cuttings in fall so roots establish through the rainy season, into lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun.

directions: Site 'Victoria' in full sun on a slope or berm with excellent drainage, since this hybrid of Ceanothus impressus is among the hardier and more forgiving California lilacs but still resents wet feet. Dense, small, glossy dark-green leaves cover a bushy, rounded frame that disappears each spring beneath a heavy, nearly continuous sheet of small, vivid indigo-blue flower clusters. It tolerates light, infrequent supplemental water better than many ceanothus species without sacrificing bloom, making it a dependable choice for mixed dry gardens as well as native plantings. Shear lightly right after flowering to keep growth dense; avoid cutting into bare old wood, which will not resprout.

common_name: Yankee Point Ceanothus (Low Spreading California Lilac Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from cuttings in fall into fertile, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in full sun; fall planting lets roots spread widely before summer heat arrives.

directions: Give 'Yankee Point' plenty of horizontal room, since this fast, low, mounding selection of Carmel ceanothus is grown expressly as a large-scale groundcover and slope stabilizer rather than an upright shrub. Glossy dark-green foliage stays dense and weed-suppressing at knee height or below while spreading branches root as they touch the ground, and small clusters of medium-blue flowers cover the plant in mid to late spring. It is unusually garden-tolerant for a ceanothus, accepting average garden watering better than most species, though established plants still perform best with infrequent, deep irrigation. Avoid foot traffic and heavy pruning into old wood, which the plant does not reliably resprout from.
scientific_name_note: Also sold as Ceanothus thyrsiflorus var. griseus 'Yankee Point' under current taxonomic treatments.

common_name: Point Reyes Ceanothus (Low Evergreen California Lilac Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from cuttings in fall into well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; afternoon shade is beneficial in hot inland gardens.

directions: Use Point Reyes ceanothus as a dense, mat-forming evergreen groundcover on banks and slopes, where its leathery, holly-like leaves and low, spreading branches root readily wherever they touch soil, helping to control erosion. Rounded clusters of violet-blue flowers open in mid-spring against the dark foliage, drawing bees and other pollinators to an otherwise low, textural planting. Coastal gardens can grow it in full sun, but in hot interior climates give it light afternoon shade to keep foliage from scorching. Once established it needs little to no summer irrigation and resents heavy, poorly drained soil.

common_name: Julia Phelps Ceanothus (Small-Leaf Indigo-Blue California Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from cuttings in fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants need little to no summer water.

directions: Grow 'Julia Phelps' as an upright, adaptable evergreen background shrub where its small, dark, textured leaves can set off dense clusters of intensely fragrant, deep indigo-blue flowers that blanket the plant in mid-spring. This long-popular hybrid tolerates pruning better than many wild ceanothus, so it can be shaped or kept lower with an occasional light trim just after bloom, but it should never be cut into bare wood. Full sun and sharp drainage are essential, as the deep root system that makes it so drought tolerant is also quick to rot in heavy or over-irrigated soil. Bees and other pollinators visit it heavily during its bloom period.
scientific_name_note: Sometimes listed as Ceanothus x pallidus 'Julia Phelps'.

common_name: Mahala Mat Ceanothus (Prostrate Mountain California Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, fast-draining, gravelly or granitic soil in full sun; this high-elevation native is adapted to cold winters with snow cover and dry summers.

directions: Mahala mat forms a dense, woody, ankle-high carpet native to the pine and mixed-conifer forests of the Sierra Nevada, Cascades, and Klamath Mountains, where it spreads by rooting stems across open, gravelly ground. Small, oval, spine-toothed evergreen leaves hug the soil, and in late spring the mat is dotted with small clusters of blue to lavender flowers that draw native bees. Unlike many lowland ceanothus, it is genuinely cold-hardy and expects a distinct dry summer dormancy paired with winter moisture, so avoid rich soil or regular irrigation once it is established. It excels as a slow but tenacious erosion-control groundcover on sunny slopes and rock gardens with sharp drainage.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Longin Russian Sage (Narrow Upright Non-Flopping Russian Sage)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Longin' needs the same excellent drainage as the species to avoid winter crown rot.

directions: 'Longin' is a stiffly upright, narrow selection of Russian sage bred for a formal, columnar habit that holds its shape without staking or flopping open, making it useful for tighter spaces than the species allows. Finely cut, aromatic, silvery-gray leaves clothe square stems topped from midsummer into fall with slender spikes of pale lavender-blue flowers that are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators. Because its narrow profile takes up less lateral space, it can be planted closer together than looser cultivars for a hedge-like screen or repeated vertical accent in a dry border. Cut the stems back hard to a low woody framework in early spring, after the coldest weather has passed, to encourage fresh, dense growth.
